title: Semicolons, colons, hyphens, parentheses, dashes and ellipses
blurb: Use semicolons and colons only where a full sentence allows them, hyphenate compound modifiers, and handle dashes, parentheses and ellipses correctly.
question: An email to new hires says, “Orientation includes: a tour, a safety class, and a badge photo for full time staff, please arrive by 7:45; because parking is limited.” Which marks are wrong, and what should replace them?

teach.body: Formally, a semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses (or separates series items that already contain commas); a colon follows a complete independent clause to introduce a list, an explanation, an example or a quotation; a hyphen joins words into one unit; dashes and parentheses set off extra information; an ellipsis marks words left out. Plain English: a semicolon needs a full sentence on BOTH sides, a colon needs one BEFORE it, and a hyphen glues words that work as one describing word.

teach.caption: Both marks need a complete sentence before them. Only the semicolon also needs one after.

head: Job
Example
rows: The lab closed early; the samples wait until tomorrow.
The road was icy; however, the van arrived.
Boise, Idaho; Reno, Nevada; and Provo, Utah
teach.caption: Conjunctive adverbs: however, therefore, moreover, consequently, nevertheless, furthermore, otherwise, thus, instead, meanwhile.

root.label: Read only the words before the colon
root.sub: Could they stand alone as a sentence?

children.label: Colon is allowed
children.sub: Bring three items: ID, login, pen.

children.edge: No: ends in a verb, preposition or “such as”
children.label: Delete the colon
children.sub: The kit includes gauze and tape.

teach.caption: Conventional colons need no test: times (10:30), ratios (3:1), business salutations (Dear Dr. Patel:).

head: Rule
Hyphen
No hyphen
rows: the child is two years old
Prefix before a capital or number
teach.caption: A hyphen is the short mark that joins words. The longer dash sets off a break; it never joins words.

rows.label: Example
values: A pair of dashes around “gauze, tape, and gloves”

teach.caption: A pair of dashes or parentheses works like a pair of commas: open it and close it. Never open with a dash and close with a comma.

teach.body: Parentheses hold supplementary information: an aside, a definition, a number or an abbreviation (“the emergency department (ED)”). The main sentence's own punctuation goes OUTSIDE the closing parenthesis: “Take one tablet (with food).” Only when a whole sentence stands inside the parentheses does its period go inside: “(Bring your card.)” Never put a comma before an opening parenthesis. Brackets are different: they mark the writer's own words inserted into a quotation (“He [the patient] refused.”).

An ellipsis is three periods ( ... ) that show words have been removed from a quotation. Quoting “The vaccine, which was tested for two years, is safe for adults” without the middle clause gives “The vaccine ... is safe for adults.” Leaving words out silently changes the quotation, so the ellipsis is required. In dialogue, an ellipsis can also show a voice trailing off: “I thought the lab was open ...”

Andre Wilson, a nursing applicant working as a unit clerk, rewrites: “Orientation has three parts: a tour, a safety class, and a badge photo for full-time staff. Please arrive by 7:45 because parking is limited.” “Includes:” put a colon after a verb, so he makes the clause complete first. Full-time comes before the noun staff, so it takes a hyphen. The comma between two sentences was a splice, so he uses a period, and the semicolon before a dependent clause goes.

teach.text: HESI A2 favorites: a semicolon before a dependent clause (“Because it rained; we stayed”), a colon straight after “are,” “include” or “such as,” a hyphen after an -ly adverb (“highly-trained”), a hyphenated age after the noun (“five-years-old”), and a comma placed before an opening parenthesis.

items: Semicolon: a complete sentence on both sides, or between series items that contain commas.
Colon: only after a complete sentence; never straight after a verb, preposition or “such as.”
Hyphenate a compound modifier before a noun, but not after it and never after an -ly adverb.
Dashes emphasize; parentheses play down; both come in pairs around mid-sentence extras.
Sentence punctuation goes outside the closing parenthesis unless a whole sentence is inside.
An ellipsis marks words removed from a quotation; brackets mark words the writer added.

summary: You can now use a semicolon between independent clauses and in complex series, place a colon only after a complete clause, and hyphenate compound modifiers before a noun. You can also choose between commas, dashes and parentheses, punctuate around parentheses, and mark omissions with an ellipsis.

A.q: Which sentence about the lab is punctuated correctly?
options: The lab closed early, the samples will be tested tomorrow.
The lab closed early; the samples will be tested tomorrow.
The lab closed early; and, the samples will be tested tomorrow.
The lab closed early the samples will be tested tomorrow.
A.why: A semicolon can join two closely related independent clauses with no conjunction.

whyNot.0: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses: this is a comma splice.
whyNot.2: A comma does not follow a coordinating conjunction such as “and,” and a semicolon plus “and” is not needed here.
whyNot.3: Two independent clauses with no punctuation make a run-on.

A.q: Which sentence uses a colon correctly to introduce a list?
options: The kit contains: three items, gauze, tape, and gloves.
The kit contains three items; gauze, tape, and gloves.
The kit contains three items, such as: gauze, tape, and gloves.
The kit contains three items: gauze, tape, and gloves.
A.why: “The kit contains three items” is a complete independent clause, so a colon may introduce the list.

whyNot.0: A colon cannot come straight after the verb “contains.”
whyNot.1: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it; a list is not one.

A.q: Which sentence about a new hire uses hyphens correctly?
options: She is a well-known nurse who works a full-time schedule.
She is a well known nurse who works a full-time schedule.
She is a well-known nurse who works a full time schedule.
She is a well known nurse who works a full time schedule.
A.why: Both compound modifiers come before a noun (nurse, schedule), so both take hyphens.

whyNot.1: “Well-known” comes before the noun “nurse,” so it needs a hyphen.
whyNot.2: “Full-time” comes before the noun “schedule,” so it needs a hyphen.
whyNot.3: Both compound modifiers come before a noun, so both need hyphens.

B.q: Which sentence correctly punctuates a series of cities and states?
options: The tour visits Boise, Idaho, Reno, Nevada, and Provo, Utah.
The tour visits Boise; Idaho; Reno; Nevada; and Provo; Utah.
The tour visits Boise, Idaho; Reno, Nevada; and Provo, Utah.
The tour visits: Boise, Idaho; Reno, Nevada; and Provo, Utah.
B.why: When series items already contain commas, semicolons separate the items.

whyNot.0: With commas only, the reader cannot tell where each city-state item ends.
whyNot.1: Semicolons separate the items, not each city from its own state.
whyNot.3: A colon cannot come straight after the verb “visits.”

B.q: A student quotes “The clinic, which opened in 1998, serves three counties” but leaves out the middle clause. Which version is correct?
options: “The clinic, serves three counties.”
“The clinic ... serves three counties.”
“The clinic serves three counties.”
“The clinic; serves three counties.”
B.why: An ellipsis shows exactly where words were removed from the quotation.

whyNot.0: The omission is not marked, and the comma now splits the subject from its verb.
whyNot.2: Words were removed without any mark, so the reader cannot tell the quotation was shortened.
whyNot.3: A semicolon cannot sit between a subject and its verb, and it does not mark an omission.

B.q: Which sentence punctuates the added information correctly?
options: Bring your ID (a driver's license or passport to the test center).
Bring your ID (a driver's license or passport.) to the test center.
Bring your ID, (a driver's license or passport) to the test center.
Bring your ID (a driver's license or passport) to the test center.
B.why: The parentheses enclose only the extra information, and no extra punctuation is added inside or before them.

whyNot.0: The closing parenthesis swallows part of the main sentence (“to the test center”).
whyNot.1: A period does not go inside a parenthetical in the middle of a sentence.
whyNot.2: A comma does not go before an opening parenthesis.

C.q: Which sentence about a pediatric aide uses hyphens correctly?
options: The newly-hired aide cared for a three-year-old boy.
The newly hired aide cared for a three year old boy.
The newly hired aide cared for a three-year-old boy.
The newly hired aide cared for a boy who is three-years-old.
C.why: Two rules: no hyphen after an -ly adverb (newly hired), and an age used before a noun is hyphenated (three-year-old boy).

whyNot.0: An adverb ending in -ly is not joined to the next word with a hyphen.
whyNot.1: “Three-year-old” comes before the noun “boy,” so it needs hyphens.
whyNot.3: After the noun, the age takes no hyphens: “three years old.”

C.q: Which revision correctly punctuates this sentence? “The pharmacy was out of the medication, therefore the nurse called the doctor.”
options: The pharmacy was out of the medication, therefore, the nurse called the doctor.
The pharmacy was out of the medication; therefore the nurse, called the doctor.
The pharmacy was out of the medication; therefore, the nurse called the doctor.
The pharmacy was out of the medication: therefore; the nurse called the doctor.
C.why: “Therefore” is a conjunctive adverb joining two clauses: semicolon before it, comma after it.

whyNot.0: Commas alone around “therefore” still leave a comma splice.
whyNot.1: The comma after “nurse” splits the subject from its verb.
whyNot.3: The colon and semicolon are reversed and misused; a semicolon belongs before “therefore.”

C.q: Which sentence uses a colon INCORRECTLY?
options: Bring items such as: your ID, your login, and a pen.
The orientation for all new staff begins at 10:30 on Tuesday.
One thing mattered most to the team: sleep.
The ratio of nurses to patients on the unit was 1:4.
C.why: A colon cannot follow “such as”; the words before it are not a complete clause.

whyNot.1: Colons are conventional in times such as 10:30.
whyNot.2: A complete clause comes before the colon, which introduces an explanation.
whyNot.3: Colons are conventional in ratios such as 1:4.

reteach.title: The semicolon is a balance scale
reteach.question: Picture a semicolon as a scale that balances only two equal weights, a colon as a spotlight pointing forward, and a hyphen as glue. What has to be true for each one to work?

blocks.body: A semicolon is a scale: put a full sentence on each pan and it balances (“It rained; we stayed inside.”). Put a fragment on one pan (“Because it rained; we stayed”) and it tips over. A colon is a spotlight: a full sentence stands behind it and shines on whatever comes next (“One thing mattered: sleep.”). A hyphen is glue: it sticks words together into one describing word before a noun (a full-time job), but once the words come after the noun (the job is full time), there is nothing to glue.

blocks.text: If the words before a colon end in “are,” “include,” “such as” or a preposition, the spotlight has no one behind it: delete the colon.

explain.body: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, comes before a conjunctive adverb (with a comma after it), or separates series items that contain commas. It does not introduce a list and does not sit next to a dependent clause.

head: Use
Example
rows: She was tired; however, she stayed.

test.q: Which sentence about the tired nurse uses a semicolon correctly?
options: The nurse, who works nights; is on call.
Although the nurse was tired; she stayed.
The nurse was tired; but stayed late.
The nurse was tired; she stayed late.
test.why: Both sides are independent clauses with their own subjects and verbs.

whyNot.0: The semicolon separates the subject from its verb and closes a comma pair incorrectly.
whyNot.1: “Although the nurse was tired” is a dependent clause.
whyNot.2: “But stayed late” has no subject, so it is not an independent clause.

explain.body: A colon follows a complete clause and introduces a list, explanation, example or quotation. Do not place it straight after a verb (are, include), a preposition, or “such as.”

rows.label: List
values: She has three: A, B, and C.
Her three are: A, B, and C.

test.q: Which sentence about favorite subjects uses a colon correctly?
options: Her favorite subjects are: biology, chemistry, and math.
Her favorite subjects include: biology, chemistry, and math.
She has three favorite subjects: biology, chemistry, and math.
She has three favorite: subjects biology, chemistry, and math.
test.why: “She has three favorite subjects” is a complete clause, so the colon may introduce the list.

whyNot.0: A colon cannot come straight after the verb “are.”
whyNot.1: A colon cannot come straight after the verb “include.”
whyNot.3: The colon splits the phrase “favorite subjects,” and the words before it are not a complete clause.

explain.body: A dash marks a sudden break or adds emphasis. A pair of dashes works like a pair of commas or parentheses but is more emphatic, and it is especially useful when the inserted part already contains commas. Do not confuse the dash with the shorter hyphen, which joins words (a well-known doctor).

rows.label: Job
values: Sets off a break or extra

test.q: Laila writes, “The kit, gauze, tape, and gloves, is ready.” The commas make the list confusing. Which punctuation should replace the two outer commas to set the list off with strong emphasis?
options: A pair of semicolons
A pair of dashes
A pair of hyphens
A colon after kit
test.why: A pair of dashes sets off an inserted list that contains commas, and it adds emphasis.

whyNot.0: Semicolons separate independent clauses or complex series items; they cannot enclose an insertion.
whyNot.2: Hyphens join words; they do not set off phrases.
whyNot.3: A colon after “kit” would need a complete clause before it and would leave “is ready” stranded.

explain.body: Parentheses add supplementary information quietly. The main sentence's punctuation stays outside the closing parenthesis, unless an entire sentence sits inside the parentheses.

test.q: Which sentence about the orientation schedule is punctuated correctly?
options: The orientation lasts 210 minutes (three and a half hours).
The orientation lasts 210 minutes (three and a half hours.)
The orientation lasts 210 minutes, (three and a half hours).
The orientation lasts (210 minutes three and a half hours).
test.why: The parenthetical is part of a larger sentence, so the sentence's period goes outside the closing parenthesis.

whyNot.1: The period belongs to the whole sentence, so it goes outside the parenthesis.
whyNot.2: A comma does not go before an opening parenthesis.
whyNot.3: The main information (210 minutes) is trapped inside the parentheses with the aside.

explain.body: Hyphenate a compound modifier before a noun (a part-time job) but not after it (the job is part time), never after an -ly adverb, and in the numbers twenty-one to ninety-nine.

test.q: Which sentence about a student's job uses hyphens correctly?
options: The student is twenty one and works a part-time job.
The student is twenty-one and works a part-time job.
The student is twenty-one and works a part time job.
The student is twenty one and works a part time job.
test.why: Twenty-one is a compound number from 21 to 99, and part-time comes before the noun job, so both take hyphens.

whyNot.0: Compound numbers from twenty-one to ninety-nine take a hyphen.
whyNot.2: “Part-time” comes before the noun “job,” so it needs a hyphen.
whyNot.3: Both the compound number and the compound modifier need hyphens.
